pass1.sentence: The NHS says 999 is for life-threatening emergencies and NHS 111 for urgent problems or when unsure, with pharmacies, GPs and urgent care centres for others.

pass1.sentence: The NHS advises calling 999 for life-threatening emergencies, such as a suspected heart attack, a suspected stroke or severe bleeding.

pass1.sentence: NHS 111 can be used online or by phone, at any time, when help is needed urgently but the situation is not life-threatening, or when it is unclear where to go.

pass1.sentence: NHS 111 gives urgent medical advice when a situation is not life-threatening.

pass1.sentence: It can be reached online at 111.nhs.uk, by phone, or through the NHS App.
pass1.note: 111 online, calling 111, or NHS App

pass1.sentence: It runs 24 hours a day, every day of the year, and calls are free from mobiles and landlines.

pass1.sentence: NHS 111 can also direct people to other services, so that they reach the right place first time.

pass1.sentence: The adviser first asks for basic details, such as who is calling, where they are, and whether the call is about themselves or another person.

pass1.sentence: Next come questions about the symptoms, including when they began, how they affect the person, and what has been tried already.

pass1.sentence: The answers lead to one of several outcomes, including an ambulance, a referral to urgent care or a GP, an out-of-hours appointment, a call back from a nurse, or advice on caring for the problem at home.
